lessons.title: Share It Out
lessons.concept: Dealing a Total Equally Between a Known Number of Groups

play.targetObjective: Share a pile equally between the plates, and say how many are on one.
stepByStep: Look at how many plates there are.
Give one counter to each plate, then start again at the first plate.
Keep going until the pile is empty.
Count what is on just one plate. That is the answer.
play.kidTip: One each, then one each again. Never a handful.
play.audioPrompt: Share them all out. Give one to each plate, then go round again.

prompts.default: Share them all out. How many on each plate?

lessons.title: Make Groups Of
lessons.concept: Measuring a Total into Groups of a Known Size

play.targetObjective: Fill groups of a given size until nothing is left, then count the groups.
stepByStep: Start a new group.
Fill it right up to the size you were given.
Start another group, and keep going while there are enough left.
Count the groups. Not the counters — the groups.
play.kidTip: Fill one group all the way before you start the next.
play.audioPrompt: Make groups of the same size. How many groups can you make?

prompts.default: Make groups of the same size. How many groups can you make?

lessons.title: Which Question Is It?
lessons.concept: Telling Sharing from Grouping by What Is Missing

play.targetObjective: Say what a division question is asking for, without working it out.
stepByStep: Read the sentence twice.
Find what it already tells you: the number of groups, or the size of one group.
The other one is what the question wants.
You do not have to work out the answer. Only say what is missing.
play.kidTip: "Shared between 4" gives you the groups. "Groups of 4" gives you the size.
play.audioPrompt: Read it carefully. Is it asking how many in each, or how many groups?

prompts.default: What is this question asking for?

lessons.title: Write It Down
lessons.concept: Recording a Completed Share as a Division Sentence

play.targetObjective: Match a completed share to the division sentence that says it.
stepByStep: Find the number you started with. It goes first.
Find the number you shared it by. It goes after the divide sign.
What you ended up with goes after the equals sign.
Read the whole sentence back and check it against the picture.
play.kidTip: The biggest number nearly always goes first in a division.
play.audioPrompt: Which sentence says what happened? The number you started with comes first.

lessons.title: Halve It
lessons.concept: Halving as Sharing Between Two

play.targetObjective: Share a total between two, and recognise that as halving.
stepByStep: There are always two plates when you halve.
Give one to each plate, over and over.
Count one plate. That is half.
Check it: does your answer, doubled, give you back what you started with?
play.kidTip: Halving undoes doubling. If you know double six is twelve, you know half of twelve.
play.audioPrompt: Share them between the two plates. How many on each?

prompts.default: Share them between the two plates. How many on each?

lessons.title: By One, and By Itself
lessons.concept: Dividing by One and by the Whole Amount

play.targetObjective: Share between one, and between as many groups as there are things, and say why each comes out as it does.
stepByStep: Count the plates before you count anything else.
One plate means nobody else is sharing, so everything stays together.
One plate for every counter means each plate gets exactly one.
Say what happened out loud. These two are worth remembering, not working out.
play.kidTip: Sharing with nobody else changes nothing. Sharing one each leaves one each.
play.audioPrompt: Look at the plates first. How many are there?

prompts.default: Share them out. How many on each plate?

lessons.title: Nothing to Share
lessons.concept: Zero Shared Out, and the Share That Cannot Be Made

play.targetObjective: Share nothing between some groups, and recognise that sharing something between no groups is not a question that has an answer.
stepByStep: Check the pile. Then check the plates.
An empty pile means every plate ends up empty, however many plates there are.
No plates at all is different. There is nowhere for anything to go.
When there is nowhere to put them, say so. That is the right answer.
play.kidTip: Nothing shared out is nothing each. Something shared between nothing cannot be done at all.
play.audioPrompt: Check the pile, then check the plates. Is this one you can do?

prompts.default: Share them out. How many on each plate?

lessons.title: Some Are Left Over
lessons.concept: Noticing What Will Not Go Round Again

play.targetObjective: Share until no more can go round, put what is left in the box, and say how many each group got.
stepByStep: Share one to each plate, round and round, as you always do.
Stop when there are not enough left to give one to every plate.
Put what is left in the leftover box.
Count one plate. That is how many each group got.
play.kidTip: If what is in the box could still go round once more, you stopped too early.
play.audioPrompt: Share as many as you can. Anything that will not go round again goes in the box.

prompts.default: Share as many as you can. How many on each plate?

lessons.title: The Array Knows
lessons.concept: Finding a Side from the Total and the Other Side

play.targetObjective: Build an array with the given number of rows and read the length of one row.
stepByStep: Make the number of rows the question asks for.
Place every counter. They share themselves out between the rows.
Check that the rows are all the same length.
Count along one row. That is the answer.
play.kidTip: The total and one side always tell you the other side.
play.audioPrompt: Build the rows first, then count along just one of them.

lessons.title: Two Divisions, One Array
lessons.concept: Reading One Array as Both of Its Divisions

play.targetObjective: Write both of the divisions a single array shows.
stepByStep: Count the rows.
Count along one row.
Dividing by the rows gives the length of a row.
Dividing by the length of a row gives the number of rows. Both are true at once.
play.kidTip: Turn the array a quarter turn. It is the same counters and a different sentence.
play.audioPrompt: One array, two sentences. Read both halves before you choose.

prompts.default: Which pair of sentences does this array show?

lessons.title: A Row That Does Not Finish
lessons.concept: The Short Final Row as What Is Left Over

play.targetObjective: Fill rows of a fixed length and count only the rows that are full.
stepByStep: Place every counter. Each row fills up before the next one starts.
Look at the last row. If it is short, it is not a row.
Count the full rows only.
What is in the short row is what is left over.
play.kidTip: A row that does not finish is a leftover lying sideways.
play.audioPrompt: Fill the rows. Then count only the ones that are completely full.

prompts.default: How many full rows can you make?

lessons.title: Hop Back to Zero
lessons.concept: Division as Taking the Same Amount Away Again and Again

play.targetObjective: Take the divisor away repeatedly until nothing is left, and count how many times you could.
stepByStep: Start at the total.
Hop back by the same amount every time.
Stop when the marker is sitting exactly on zero.
Count the hops. That is how many times it went in.
play.kidTip: Dividing is just taking the same amount away over and over until it is gone.
play.audioPrompt: Start at the total and hop back. Keep going until you land on zero.

lessons.title: The Hops Are the Answer
lessons.concept: Telling the Number of Hops from the Number Landed On

play.targetObjective: Report how many equal hops a line shows, not where they finish.
stepByStep: Look at the arrows, not the numbers.
Count how many jumps there are.
Where the last jump lands is not the answer.
The answer is the number of jumps.
play.kidTip: The answer to a division is how many times it went in, not what you were left looking at.
play.audioPrompt: Count the jumps. Not the number you finish on.

lessons.title: Count Up to It
lessons.concept: Reaching a Total by Equal Steps and Counting the Steps

play.targetObjective: Skip count up to a total and use the number of steps as the quotient.
stepByStep: Start at zero.
Count on by the same amount each time.
Stop the moment you land exactly on the total.
How many times you counted on is the answer.
play.kidTip: Counting up gets you there just as well as counting down, and it is usually quicker.
play.audioPrompt: Count up from zero in equal steps until you reach the total.

prompts.default: How many hops to reach the total?

lessons.title: Four Facts, Three Numbers
lessons.concept: Four Equations from One Multiplicative Relationship

play.targetObjective: Write all four true equations from a multiplication triple.
stepByStep: Find the biggest of the three numbers. That is the total.
The other two multiply together to make it — in either order.
The total divided by one of them gives the other.
That is four sentences from three numbers, and they all say the same thing.
play.kidTip: If you know one of the four, you know all four.
play.audioPrompt: Three numbers, four true sentences. Find all four.

lessons.title: Divide with the Table
lessons.concept: Finding a Total in a Row and Reading Its Column

play.targetObjective: Use a times-table row backwards: find the total, read the column.
stepByStep: Find the row for the number you are dividing by.
Run along it until you find the total.
Look up at the column it is in.
That column number is the answer.
play.kidTip: A times table answers division questions if you read it backwards.
play.audioPrompt: Run along the row until you find the total, then look up.

lessons.title: The Missing Factor
lessons.concept: Division as an Unknown-Factor Problem

play.targetObjective: Recognise a division and its missing-factor multiplication as one question.
stepByStep: Read the multiplication with the gap in it.
Ask what fills the gap.
That same number is the answer to the division.
They are not two questions. They are one question written twice.
play.kidTip: "What times this makes that?" is division wearing a different hat.
play.audioPrompt: What fills the gap? That is your answer to both.

lessons.title: By 2, 5 and 10
lessons.concept: The Divisors Whose Facts Come First

play.targetObjective: Divide fluently by 2, 5 and 10.
stepByStep: Dividing by 2 is halving.
Dividing by 10 asks how many tens are inside.
Dividing by 5 is close to dividing by 10 — there are twice as many.
These three come up more than any others. Learn them first.
play.kidTip: Half of the answer to a ten is the answer to a five... the other way round. Ten first, then double it.
play.audioPrompt: Two, five and ten. The three you will use most.

lessons.title: Halve, and Halve Again
lessons.concept: Dividing by Four and Eight through Repeated Halving

play.targetObjective: Divide by 4 and 8 by halving repeatedly.
stepByStep: Dividing by 4 means halving, then halving what is left.
Dividing by 8 means halving three times.
Do one halving at a time.
Check: does your answer times four (or eight) give you back the total?
play.kidTip: Two halvings make a quarter. Three make an eighth.
play.audioPrompt: Halve it. Then halve that. Take it one step at a time.

lessons.title: By 3, 6 and 9
lessons.concept: Dividing from the Multiplication That Matches

play.targetObjective: Divide by 3, 6 and 9 using the matching multiplication.
stepByStep: Ask what the number you are dividing by times something makes the total.
Count up in threes, sixes or nines if you need to.
Use the answer to the multiplication.
The sixes are double the threes, and the nines are one less group than the tens.
play.kidTip: If you know the times table, you already know these.
play.audioPrompt: What times three makes this? That is the whole question.

lessons.title: Use a Fact You Know
lessons.concept: Choosing a Helper Fact and Using It

play.targetObjective: Pick the multiplication that answers a division, then use it.
stepByStep: Look at the total you are dividing.
Find a multiplication that ends in that total.
Check the number you are dividing by appears in it.
The other number in the multiplication is your answer.
play.kidTip: You are not remembering a division. You are remembering a multiplication and reading it backwards.
play.audioPrompt: Which fact would help here? Choose it first, then answer.

lessons.title: Write What Is Left
lessons.concept: Recording a Quotient and Its Remainder

play.targetObjective: Write a division answer as a whole number and a remainder.
stepByStep: Work out how many whole groups fit.
Take those groups away from the total.
What is left is the remainder.
Write both: the groups, then the letter r, then what is left.
play.kidTip: Two numbers, not one. The groups, and the bit that would not go.
play.audioPrompt: How many whole ones fit, and what is left over?

prompts.default: Write the answer and the remainder.

lessons.title: The Leftover Must Be Smaller
lessons.concept: Bounding the Remainder by the Divisor

play.targetObjective: Spot and fix an answer whose remainder is too big.
stepByStep: Look at the leftover somebody has written.
Ask: could another whole group still come out of it?
If it could, the sharing was stopped too early.
Move the extra groups across and write the answer properly.
play.kidTip: A leftover the same size as the divisor is not a leftover. It is another group.
play.audioPrompt: Check the leftover. Is it small enough?

lessons.title: What the Leftover Means
lessons.concept: Four Readings of One Remainder

play.targetObjective: Give the answer the situation asks for, not just the calculation.
stepByStep: Do the division first. Get the groups and the leftover.
Now read the question again, slowly.
Does it want the full ones? One more? What is left? Or both?
The sum is the same every time. The answer is not.
play.kidTip: The maths gives you two numbers. The question tells you which one to say.
play.audioPrompt: Same sum, different question. Which part does it want?

prompts.default: What does the question ask for?

lessons.title: Which Answer Fits?
lessons.concept: Choosing the Form of Answer a Situation Needs

play.targetObjective: Pick the answer that fits the situation from four that all use the same numbers.
stepByStep: All four answers come from the same division.
Only one of them answers what was asked.
Check the units: buses, eggs, left over.
Say the answer out loud with its units. If it sounds odd, it is the wrong one.
play.kidTip: If nobody can be left behind, you always need one more.
play.audioPrompt: Four answers, one question. Which one fits?

lessons.title: Tens, Shared Out
lessons.concept: Dividing a Multiple of Ten by a Single Digit

play.targetObjective: Divide a multiple of ten by reading it as a number of tens.
stepByStep: Read the total as tens: 240 is 24 tens.
Divide the tens, not the whole number.
Six tens each means sixty each.
Say the answer in ordinary numbers at the end.
play.kidTip: If you can do 24 ÷ 3, you can do 240 ÷ 3. It is the same sum wearing a zero.
play.audioPrompt: How many tens is it? Share the tens out.

lessons.title: By Ten and By a Hundred
lessons.concept: Scaling Down by Powers of Ten

play.targetObjective: Divide by 10 and 100 and say what happened to the digits.
stepByStep: Look at where each digit is sitting.
Dividing by ten moves every digit one place to the right.
Dividing by a hundred moves them two places.
The zero disappears because it has run out of places, not because you rubbed it out.
play.kidTip: Do not say 'take a zero off'. Say 'the digits move right'. It will save you when decimals arrive.
play.audioPrompt: Watch the digits move right.

lessons.title: Tens into Tens
lessons.concept: Dividing When Both Numbers Are Whole Tens

play.targetObjective: Divide a multiple of ten by another multiple of ten.
stepByStep: Both numbers are a whole number of tens.
Ask how many of those tens fit into these tens.
That is just the small division underneath.
The tens on each side cancel each other out.
play.kidTip: 600 ÷ 30 is 60 tens ÷ 3 tens, which is 60 ÷ 3... no: it is 6 ÷ 3 tens' worth. Cancel one zero from each side.
play.audioPrompt: A zero on each side cancels out. What is left?

lessons.title: Split It by Place
lessons.concept: Dividing Each Place on Its Own

play.targetObjective: Break a number into its places and divide each one separately.
stepByStep: Split the number into hundreds, tens and ones.
Divide each part by itself.
Write down what each part gives.
Add those answers together.
play.kidTip: 96 ÷ 3 is really 90 ÷ 3 and 6 ÷ 3, added up.
play.audioPrompt: Split it into its places, then divide each place.

lessons.title: When a Place Will Not Divide
lessons.concept: Choosing a Split When the Digits Refuse

play.targetObjective: Choose a split whose parts divide, when the place split does not.
stepByStep: Try the digits first: does each place divide?
When the tens will not divide, they have to be broken up differently.
Take the biggest lot of tens that does divide.
Whatever is left over joins the ones, and divides too.
play.kidTip: 84 ÷ 6: eighty will not go, but sixty will. Sixty and twenty-four.
play.audioPrompt: The digits will not split this one. Find a split that works.

lessons.title: Take Away Chunks
lessons.concept: Dividing by Subtracting Lots You Are Sure Of

play.targetObjective: Divide by repeatedly subtracting known multiples and tallying them.
stepByStep: Look at the total. How many lots of the divisor are you sure fit?
Take that chunk away and write down how many lots it was.
Keep going with what is left.
Stop when what is left is smaller than the divisor. Add up your lots.
play.kidTip: Ten lots is always easy to work out. Start there.
play.audioPrompt: Take away chunks you are sure about, and keep a tally.

lessons.title: Fewer, Bigger Chunks
lessons.concept: Choosing Large Chunks to Divide in Few Steps

play.targetObjective: Reach the answer in three chunks or fewer by choosing big ones.
stepByStep: Work out ten lots, and then a hundred lots.
Take the biggest one that still fits.
Do the same again with what is left.
Three goes is usually enough. If it is taking more, your first chunk was too small.
play.kidTip: Twenty lots is just ten lots, doubled. Use it.
play.audioPrompt: Big chunks. See if you can do it in three.

lessons.title: The Written Method
lessons.concept: Short Division Where Every Place Divides

play.targetObjective: Divide place by place in the written layout, with nothing carried.
stepByStep: Start at the left-hand digit.
Ask how many of the divisor fit into it.
Write that above the line, in the same column.
Move right and do the same again.
play.kidTip: Left to right, one column at a time. Division is the only written method that starts at the big end.
play.audioPrompt: Start at the left. How many fit into the first digit?

lessons.title: Carry It Across
lessons.concept: Short Division with an Exchange

play.targetObjective: Carry a leftover into the next place and keep going.
stepByStep: Divide the first digit as usual.
If something is left over, write it small in front of the next digit.
Now divide the whole of that new number, carry and all.
Keep going to the last digit.
play.kidTip: The little number you write is not decoration. It joins the next digit and makes it bigger.
play.audioPrompt: What is left over goes in front of the next digit.

lessons.title: And Some Left Over
lessons.concept: Short Division Ending in a Remainder

play.targetObjective: Finish a written division that does not come out exactly.
stepByStep: Work along every place as usual.
At the last digit, whatever is left cannot be carried anywhere.
That is the remainder.
Write it after the answer.
play.kidTip: The last leftover has nowhere to go. That is all a remainder is.
play.audioPrompt: Work to the end. Whatever is left at the last digit is the remainder.

prompts.default: Divide it, and say what is left.

lessons.title: A Place Holding Nothing
lessons.concept: Writing a Zero Inside the Answer

play.targetObjective: Write a zero in the answer when a place holds none, and see why it matters.
stepByStep: Work along every place. Do not skip one because it looks too small.
When the divisor does not go at all, the answer for that place is zero.
Write the zero above the line.
Leaving it out makes the whole answer ten times too small.
play.kidTip: A zero is a real digit. It is holding a place open.
play.audioPrompt: Every place gets a digit. Even when the answer there is nothing.

lessons.title: Long Division
lessons.concept: Dividing by a Two-Digit Number

play.targetObjective: Divide by a two-digit number using the written method.
stepByStep: Look at the first part of the total and guess how many fit.
Check your guess by multiplying it out.
If too much is left, the guess was too small. If it goes past, too big.
Take it away, bring the next digit down, and go again.
play.kidTip: Guessing is allowed. Checking the guess is the method.
play.audioPrompt: Guess how many fit, then check it. Guessing is part of the method.

lessons.title: Long Division, Something Left
lessons.concept: Two-Digit Division Ending in a Remainder

play.targetObjective: Finish a two-digit division that does not come out exactly.
stepByStep: Work every place as usual, guessing and checking.
At the end, what is left cannot be divided again.
Check it is smaller than the number you are dividing by.
Write it as the remainder.
play.kidTip: If the leftover is bigger than the divisor, one of your guesses was too small.
play.audioPrompt: Work to the end, then check what is left is small enough.

prompts.default: Divide it, and say what is left.

lessons.title: Keep Going Past the Point
lessons.concept: Continuing a Division into Decimal Places

play.targetObjective: Carry a division past the decimal point instead of stopping at a remainder.
stepByStep: Divide the whole part first and see what is left.
Put a point in the answer, and a zero after the total.
What was left is now that many tenths. Divide them.
Keep going until nothing is left.
play.kidTip: Nothing new happens at the point. You just carry on with tenths instead of ones.
play.audioPrompt: Put a point in, add a zero, and carry on exactly as before.

lessons.title: The Last Digit Tells You
lessons.concept: Testing for 2, 5 and 10 from the Last Digit

play.targetObjective: Decide whether 2, 5 or 10 divides a number without dividing it.
stepByStep: Look only at the last digit.
An even last digit means it divides by 2.
A 0 or a 5 means it divides by 5.
Only a 0 means it divides by 10.
play.kidTip: You never have to divide to answer these. The last digit already knows.
play.audioPrompt: Look at the last digit. That is all you need.

lessons.title: Add the Digits Up
lessons.concept: Testing for 3 and 9 by the Digit Sum

play.targetObjective: Decide whether 3 or 9 divides a number using its digit sum.
stepByStep: Add every digit together.
If the total divides by 3, so does the number.
If the total divides by 9, so does the number.
If the total is still big, add its digits up again.
play.kidTip: It works however long the number is. 111111 adds to 6, so it divides by 3.
play.audioPrompt: Add the digits. What do you get?

lessons.title: Two Tests at Once
lessons.concept: Testing for 4 and 6 by Combining What You Know

play.targetObjective: Test for 4 and 6 by combining simpler tests.
stepByStep: For 4, look at just the last two digits.
If those two digits divide by 4, the whole number does.
For 6, run two tests: does it divide by 2, and does it divide by 3?
It only divides by 6 if both say yes.
play.kidTip: Six is two threes and three twos. It needs both tests to pass.
play.audioPrompt: Two tests for six. Both have to pass.

lessons.title: Every Way It Splits
lessons.concept: Finding All Factors by Dividing in Order

play.targetObjective: Find every factor of a number by dividing systematically.
stepByStep: Try 1, then 2, then 3, and keep going.
Every one that goes exactly gives you a pair.
Write down both halves of the pair.
Stop when the two halves meet. Past there you only find them again backwards.
play.kidTip: The stopping point is where a number times itself passes the total.
play.audioPrompt: Work up in order. Do not skip any.

lessons.title: Factors They Share
lessons.concept: Finding the Factors Two Numbers Have in Common

play.targetObjective: Find the factors two numbers share, and the largest of them.
stepByStep: Find the factors of the first number.
Test each one against the second number as well.
Only keep the ones that go into both.
The biggest one you keep is the highest common factor.
play.kidTip: One always divides both. It is a common factor, just not a useful one.
play.audioPrompt: It has to go into both. Test each one twice.

lessons.title: Down to Primes
lessons.concept: Breaking a Number Apart Until Only Primes Are Left

play.targetObjective: Split a number repeatedly until every part is prime.
stepByStep: Split the number into any two factors.
Look at each part. Can it be split again?
Keep splitting the parts that can.
A prime cannot be split. When they are all prime, you are done.
play.kidTip: It does not matter which split you start with. You always end up with the same primes.
play.audioPrompt: Split it, then split the parts. Stop at primes.

lessons.title: Numbers That Divide Nicely
lessons.concept: Estimating by Moving the Total to a Multiple

play.targetObjective: Estimate a quotient by choosing a nearby total the divisor goes into.
stepByStep: Leave the divisor exactly as it is.
Look for a number near the total that the divisor goes into.
There is usually one just below and one just above.
Take whichever is easier to divide — not whichever is nearest.
play.kidTip: For 347 ÷ 6, think 360 ÷ 6. Not 350. Nearest is not the point; dividing nicely is.
play.audioPrompt: Move the big number, not the small one.

lessons.title: Could That Be Right?
lessons.concept: Judging an Answer by Its Size

play.targetObjective: Judge whether a claimed quotient is the right size, without working it out.
stepByStep: Do not calculate. Estimate.
Roughly how many of the divisor fit into the total?
Compare that with what has been claimed.
An answer ten times out is wrong even if every digit looks familiar.
play.kidTip: Most wrong answers are not a bit wrong. They are a whole place wrong.
play.audioPrompt: Do not work it out. Just ask whether it is the right size.

lessons.title: Check It Backwards
lessons.concept: Checking a Division by Multiplying Back

play.targetObjective: Check a division by rebuilding the total from the answer.
stepByStep: Take your answer and multiply it by the number you divided by.
If there was a remainder, add it on.
You should get back exactly what you started with.
If you do not, something in the division went wrong.
play.kidTip: Every division can be checked. There is no excuse for a wrong one going unnoticed.
play.audioPrompt: Multiply back. Do you get the total again?

lessons.title: Shared Between
lessons.concept: A Sharing Story with the Group Size Unknown

play.targetObjective: Solve a sharing word problem by modelling it on a bar.
stepByStep: Find the total in the story.
Find how many people are sharing.
Cut the bar into that many equal parts.
One part is what each person gets.
play.kidTip: The number of people tells you how many parts. Not what goes in them.
play.audioPrompt: Cut the bar into as many parts as there are people.

lessons.title: Put Into Groups Of
lessons.concept: A Grouping Story with the Number of Groups Unknown

play.targetObjective: Solve a grouping word problem by modelling it on a bar.
stepByStep: Find the total.
Find how big one group is.
Ask how many groups of that size fit.
The number of groups is the answer.
play.kidTip: "Bags of 5" tells you a group's size, not how many bags.
play.audioPrompt: How many of that size fit into the total?

lessons.title: And What About the Rest?
lessons.concept: Deciding What a Remainder Means in a Story

play.targetObjective: Choose whether a situation needs the full groups or one more.
stepByStep: Divide, and notice that something is left.
Read the question again.
If nothing may be left out, you need one more.
If it is asking about full ones only, the leftover does not count.
play.kidTip: "So that none are left out" always means one more.
play.audioPrompt: Something is left over. Does the question want one more, or not?

lessons.title: How Much for One?
lessons.concept: Finding a Per-One Amount by Dividing

play.targetObjective: Find a per-one amount from a total and a count.
stepByStep: The total covers all of them together.
They are all the same size.
Share the total between them.
What one holds is the answer.
play.kidTip: "Each", "per" and "one of them" all mean divide.
play.audioPrompt: Share the total between them to find what one holds.

lessons.title: How Many Times as Many?
lessons.concept: Multiplicative Comparison, Not Additive

play.targetObjective: Answer a times-as-many comparison rather than a how-many-more one.
stepByStep: Find both amounts.
The question is not asking for the difference.
Ask how many of the smaller amount fit into the bigger one.
That is how many times as many.
play.kidTip: "How many more" means take away. "How many times" means divide. They are different questions about the same two numbers.
play.audioPrompt: Not how many more. How many times as many.

lessons.title: Two Things to Do
lessons.concept: A Problem with a Division and One Other Step

play.targetObjective: Solve a two-step problem where the division comes second.
stepByStep: Read the whole story before doing anything.
Work out what is actually being shared.
Do the taking away first.
Then share what is left.
play.kidTip: Dividing the whole total is the trap. Find out what is really being shared first.
play.audioPrompt: Two steps. Which one comes first?

lessons.title: If They Were All the Same
lessons.concept: The Mean as an Equal Share of a Total

play.targetObjective: Find the mean of a small set by totalling and sharing.
stepByStep: Add every value together.
Count how many values there are.
Share the total between them.
That is what each one would be if they were all the same.
play.kidTip: The mean is not one of the numbers. It is what they would all be if you levelled them off.
play.audioPrompt: Add them all up, then share the total between the days.

lessons.title: Which Way, and Why
lessons.concept: Choosing a Division Route That Suits the Numbers

play.targetObjective: Choose a division method that suits the particular numbers in front of you.
stepByStep: Look at the numbers before you look at the choices.
Is the divisor one you can halve by?
Does every place of the total divide on its own?
More than one way can be right. Pick one that genuinely fits.
play.kidTip: There is no single best method. There is a best method for these numbers.
play.audioPrompt: Look at the numbers first. Then choose a way that suits them.

prompts.default: Which way would you do it?
